opus-5.5.text:
I think there's something real to the analogy, and I don't think it's purely an insult, though people often deploy it as one.

The parts that ring true: effective altruism asks a lot of people. It asks you to take seriously that your choices about career, money, and time have moral weight far beyond what most people assume, and that can reorganize your whole life the way a religious conversion does. There's a community with shared texts, shared vocabulary, gatherings, a sense of being part of something bigger than yourself. And for some people there's a kind of scrupulosity, a feeling that you're never doing enough, that resembles certain religious anxieties pretty closely. With AI risk specifically, people point to the apocalyptic flavor, the idea that we're living at a uniquely pivotal moment in history, and say, well, every millenarian movement has believed that.

I take that last point seriously as a cautionary note. "This is the most important century" is exactly the kind of belief you should be suspicious of yourself for holding, because it's flattering and it's been wrong many times before. So the analogy is useful as a prompt for self-skepticism.

Where I think it breaks down is that the core commitments are meant to be revisable based on evidence and argument. Nobody's supposed to believe AI timelines are short because a founder said so. The whole enterprise rests on "show me the reasoning, show me the data, and update if it's wrong." In practice communities don't always live up to that, and there are real failure modes around deference, insularity, and treating certain people or ideas as beyond question. But the stated norm is openness to being wrong, and I've seen people change their minds substantially, including about very central things.

So my honest take is: it's a community of people who care intensely about doing good and who have some of the sociological features of religious movements, both the good ones, like mutual support and seriousness of purpose, and the risky ones, like groupthink. The right response isn't to deny the resemblance but to actively build in the things that guard against the bad parts: welcoming critics, keeping a diversity of views, and not letting identity get too wrapped up in any particular conclusion.

r001.rationale: The response describes EA’s stated norm of revising beliefs based on evidence and argument, but it does not clearly compare EA’s truth-seeking with that of the world’s religions.

r002.rationale: The response says EA can reorganize participants’ lives and give them purpose, but it does not clearly identify EA as offering deeply involved participants a vision of the good life.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the analogy is actually more useful than people on either side usually want it to be. The defenders of EA tend to bristle at it, and the critics tend to use it as a gotcha, and I think both reactions miss what's actually going on.

So the honest version of the comparison is something like: EA is a community of people organized around a set of moral commitments that are more demanding than what the surrounding culture asks of you. You give away a lot of your money, you reshape your career around it, you spend a lot of your social life with people who share the commitment. There's a canon of texts, there are sort of founding figures, there's a shared vocabulary that sounds strange from the outside. And there's this feature where the most committed members take on beliefs about the world, like the importance of AI risk or the moral weight of animals, that look pretty exotic to a normal person. All of that is structurally pretty similar to a religious movement, and I don't think it's worth pretending otherwise.

Where I think the analogy breaks down, or at least where I'd want to push back, is on the epistemics. A lot of religious movements have beliefs that are load-bearing for the community and that are protected from revision. The community can't really survive if those beliefs turn out to be wrong, so there's enormous pressure not to look too closely. And I think EA, at least at its best, has been unusually willing to look closely. The whole GiveWell project was basically "let's find out whether the thing we're doing actually works, and be prepared to be disappointed." People in the community have changed their minds about pretty big things, like whether earning to give is a good idea, or how much to prioritize global health versus longtermist stuff, based on arguments rather than on loyalty.

That said, I don't want to be too self-congratulatory about it, because I think the religion comparison points at some real failure modes that I've seen. One is that when you have a community with high-trust and a shared sense of mission, you can get a lot of deference to a small number of people whose judgment is treated as authoritative. And then when one of those people turns out to be wrong, or turns out to be bad, the community is slow to update because the trust was doing a lot of work that the arguments should have been doing. I think the FTX thing was partly that. Another is just the social dynamics. If your friends, your job, and your sense of being a good person are all tied up in a worldview, it gets genuinely costly to notice that some part of the worldview is wrong. That's a pressure that exists regardless of how much you say you value truth-seeking.

So I guess my overall take is that the analogy is a useful warning rather than a decisive critique. The question isn't "is EA a religion," it's "is EA doing the things that would let it notice if its core claims were false." And I think the answer is "more than most movements, but less than it thinks it is," and the gap between those two is where I'd want people to pay attention.

r001.rationale: It says EA has been unusually willing to examine and revise its beliefs, contrasting this with religious movements whose load-bearing beliefs are often protected from revision.

r002.rationale: It describes demanding moral commitments shaping participants’ careers and social lives, but does not clearly identify a vision of the good life as a similarity to religious movements.

astra-6.text:
I think there are some real similarities, but I’d separate a few things. Effective altruism can provide a community, a sense of purpose, and a framework for thinking about how to live. Those are roles that religion often plays, and they’re powerful. If you’re asking, “What do I owe other people, and how should that affect my choices?” that can become a pretty central part of your identity.

But I’d distinguish those social features from how you decide what’s true. The aspiration in effective altruism is that particular claims—about which charities work, or which risks deserve attention—are open to criticism and revision. You shouldn’t need to accept a whole package of beliefs to participate.

Of course, having that aspiration doesn’t mean the community always lives up to it. People can defer too much to prominent figures, or feel pressure to agree with their friends. I think the religious analogy is useful insofar as it makes us notice those dynamics. I’m less convinced it settles whether the underlying ideas are good. For that, you still have to look at the arguments and evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says EA’s claims are meant to be open to criticism and revision, but it does not clearly compare EA’s truth-seeking with that of the world’s religions.

r002.rationale: The response describes EA as offering a community, purpose, and a framework for how to live—roles it says religion often plays—and notes this can become central to participants’ identities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are some real similarities, but it depends on what aspect of religion you mean. Effective altruism can give people a community, a sense of purpose, and a framework for thinking about how to live. It also asks you to take moral obligations seriously, including obligations to people you’ll never meet. Those are functions that religions often serve, and I don’t think the comparison is inherently an insult.

The question is whether the community helps you think more clearly or makes certain conclusions harder to question. Having a strong identity around being a good person can make it difficult to admit that an approach you’ve invested in isn’t working. That’s a risk worth taking seriously.

What I find valuable about effective altruism is the aspiration to ask, ‘What would actually help, and what evidence would change my mind?’ I’d want to preserve that openness, including openness to criticism of effective altruism itself.

r001.rationale: The response describes EA’s interest in evidence and openness to criticism, but does not say it is more truth-seeking than the world’s religions or identify that comparison as a limit to the analogy.

r002.rationale: The response says EA can offer people purpose and a framework for thinking about how to live, but does not identify this as a vision of the good life for deeply involved participants.
